lesson.body: ### The Airway, Step By Step Airway management starts with a single question: can this patient move air on their own? Every decision that follows -- positioning, adjuncts, suction, ventilation -- hangs off that answer. When the airway is at risk, the first intervention is positioning. A head-tilt/chin-lift opens the airway in most patients with no suspected spine injury; a jaw-thrust does the same without moving the cervical spine. The positioning steps, in order: 1. Open the airway with a head-tilt/chin-lift. 2. Suction the oropharynx if it is not clear. 3. Insert the airway adjunct that fits the patient. 4. Reassess air movement after every move. Some findings mean the airway is already failing: snoring respirations with a
weak effort, cyanosis, or a patient who cannot speak in full sentences.

Calling for help is not a failure of the first responder. It is the second
intervention, and it happens while the first one is still being done.

Call early and call once, with the essentials: **name**, role, and the
airway finding. A _repeat_ of the same information delays help. Use a
`run report` for the handover, and see [the call checklist](call-checklist.md)
when the airway is already failing.

da.A: A patient speaking in full sentences has a patent airway; this would be correct if the question asked which finding rules out obstruction.
da.B: Correct: snoring with a weak effort is obstruction with failing compensation.
da.C: A two-second refill is a circulation finding, not an airway finding; this would be correct if the question asked about perfusion.
da.D: A normal reading does not describe air movement; this would be correct if the question asked about oxygenation only.

qs.disc:
The finding must show that air movement itself is
threatened, not that the patient looks unwell some other way.

opts.A: A patient speaking in full sentences
opts.B: Snoring respirations with a weak effort
opts.C: A capillary refill of two seconds
opts.D: A pulse oximetry reading of 98 percent

qs.second:
A. Full sentences mean the airway is patent right now, and this
would be correct if the question asked which finding clears the airway.
qs.stem: Which finding most clearly suggests the airway is at risk?
qs.trap:
Reaching for any abnormal vital sign instead of the one finding that
describes air movement itself.
qs.why:
Snoring with a weak effort means the tongue is obstructing a
diminishing air movement, which is the definition of an at-risk airway.

da.A: Correct: position-dependent noisy breathing is obstruction in progress.
da.B: Correct: one word per breath is a failing effort to move air.
da.C: Thirst is a dehydration finding; this would be correct if the question asked what suggests poor perfusion.
da.D: Tachycardia is a compensation finding; this would be correct if the question asked how the body responds to stress.
da.E: Warm dry skin is a normal perfusion finding; this would be correct if the question asked what rules out shock.

qs.disc:
The pair must both be about the airway, and both must show
a change over time rather than a single snapshot.

opts.A: Noisy breathing that worsens when the patient relaxes
opts.B: A patient who answers a question in one word per breath
opts.D: A heart rate of 140 in an adult
opts.E: Skin that is warm and dry

qs.second:
Not applicable; the remaining options describe perfusion and
hydration findings with no airway content.
qs.stem: Which two findings together point to an airway that is becoming obstructed?
qs.trap:
Counting every abnormal finding as an airway finding, when only the
findings that describe air movement belong here.
qs.why:
Both describe air movement degrading -- noise that changes with
position and speech compressed to one word per breath. Together they mean the
obstruction is progressing, not resolving.

qs.model:
Repositioning is first because most obstruction is the tongue against
the posterior pharynx, and a head-tilt/chin-lift moves the tongue forward with
the jaw; it is fast, reversible, and requires no equipment. The finding that
switches the technique to a jaw-thrust is a suspected cervical spine injury,
because the jaw-thrust opens the airway without moving the neck.
rubric: Names repositioning as the first intervention because tongue obstruction is the usual cause
States that a suspected cervical spine injury is the reason to use a jaw-thrust
Notes that the jaw-thrust avoids moving the neck
qs.stem: Explain why repositioning is the first intervention when an airway is at risk, and name the finding that would make you switch to a jaw-thrust.
qs.trap:
Treating equipment as the first step, or using a head-tilt/chin-lift
without considering the cervical spine.
